ops.title: git >= 2.44 populates refs/remotes/origin/HEAD on fetch, so the no-trunk state is far rarer than it looks
ops.body:
Measured on git 2.55.0 (2026-08-03). The common wisdom that "`git remote add`
sets no `origin/HEAD` until you run `git remote set-head`" is only half true on
modern git:

- A repo built with `git remote add` + push genuinely has no
  `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`.
- But after a plain `git fetch origin`, `git symbolic-ref
  refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` prints `refs/remotes/origin/main`. Git >= 2.44
  writes it during any fetch that can resolve it.

This matters wherever code reasons about `vcs.ErrNoTrunk`:

- **`ccx vcs restack` fetches BEFORE resolving trunk**, so its no-trunk refusal
  is reachable only when the fetch cannot resolve it — `remote.<name>.
  followRemoteHEAD=never` (git >= 2.47), or a remote whose own HEAD names a
  branch it does not have. The refusal is correct and tested; it just fires far
  less often in the field than planning assumed. The `main`/`master` guess it
  replaced was already dead code for most users.
- **`ccx vcs worktree rm` does NOT fetch**, so for it the no-origin-HEAD state
  persists until something else fetches. That is the surface where the
  ErrNoTrunk policy (skip the trunk-holder guard on a proven miss) is actually
  observable — narrow, but not empty: `git remote add` with no fetch yet.
  `git clone` sets it, so cloned repos are unaffected either way.

Consequence for planning: do not size an ErrNoTrunk policy change by imagining
`git remote add` is common and permanent. Ask whether the code path fetches
first. Two ccx consumers answer that differently.
